title: 2025-01-28 Redwood security deep dive with Astra Financial
summary: Security deep-dive covering Redwood Private deployment architectures (VPC and on-prem), encryption/KMS options, RBAC/SSO integration, audit logging, data residency, and network isolation (ingress/egress and firewalling). Customer requested SOC2 evidence, detailed network diagram, and proposed pilot plan for an air-gapped PoC.
next_steps: Samir to share SOC 2 Type II report and ISO docs by 2025-02-03
Leah to provide detailed network diagram and recommended firewall rules by 2025-02-05
Customer to schedule follow-up architecture workshop (2 hours) week of 2025-02-10
Maya to propose pilot packaging and on-prem checklist for air-gapped PoC
action_items: Samir - share SOC2 and compliance pack (2025-02-03)
Leah - network diagram + k8s/VLAN mapping and firewall rule suggestions (2025-02-05)
Maya - draft on-prem air-gap deploy checklist and expected infra footprint (2025-02-06)
Priya/Mark - confirm internal stakeholders and compliance acceptance criteria (2025-02-07)
transcript: 00:00 Samir Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're going to run through a security deep dive for Redwood Private and the VPC/on-prem architecture. We have Leah and Maya from our team. Could you quick intros from Astra? 00:07 Mark Johnson: Mark here, CISO at Astra. Priya and Daniel are on from infra, Aisha from compliance. 00:12 Leah Chen: Great, thanks. Agenda: SOC2/ISO evidence, RBAC and SSO, audit logs & retention, encryption/KMS, then deep-dive on network isolation, ingress/egress and firewalling. We'll leave time for Q&A. 00:25 Priya Kapoor: Sounds good. We're especially concerned about ingress/egress and the ability to run an air-gapped PoC in our on-prem colo. 00:31 Maya Rodriguez: Perfect, that's something we've done with other financials, so we'll walk through options. 00:36 Daniel Ruiz: Quick note — our network team requires port-level rules and IPS/IDS integration; we also want to understand how Redwood's runtime handles outbound calls. 00:45 Leah Chen: Right, so quick overview: Redwood Private can be deployed in three main patterns — dedicated VPC in your cloud account, private control plane + customer data plane in a VPC, or fully on-prem air-gapped where control plane is local. For each we support SAML SSO, RBAC mappings, and KMS integrations. 01:05 Mark Johnson: When you say "KMS integrations" — do you integrate with our HSM or just cloud KMS? We need FIPS 140-2-compatible key management. 01:14 Samir Patel: We support cloud KMS (AWS KMS, Google KMS, Azure KeyVault) and bring-your-own-key (BYOK) via KMS/HSM connectors. For on-prem we can integrate with an HSM provider over PKCS#11 or KMIP — there's some configuration work but it's supported. 01:28 Aisha Bello: And your encryption at rest defaults? Full disk, DB-level, object store? 01:34 Leah Chen: Data at rest is encrypted using AES-256. For Private we can encrypt model artifacts and persistent stores using your KMS keys. For object storage we support server-side encryption with customer-managed keys. There was a small note: sometimes the transcription says "AES 265" on older notes — sorry for the OCR, but it's AES-256. 01:51 Daniel Ruiz: Walk me through key rotation — do you rotate automatically or do we control rotation schedules? 01:56 Maya Rodriguez: Key rotation can be customer-driven; we also support automatic rotation for cloud KMS per provider APIs. For HSMs we rely on your rotation procedures and we can call rotate endpoints. We'll capture specifics in the runbook. 02:12 Priya Kapoor: Audit logging — we need immutable audit logs with 7 years retention and ability to forward to our SIEM (Splunk) and to an air-gapped archive. How does Redwood handle logs from Private? 02:23 Leah Chen: For Private, audit logs are emitted locally and can be shipped to your chosen logging endpoint — syslog, Kafka, or S3. We support structured JSON logs with fields for user principal, action, resource, and request IDs. You can configure log retention and shipping; for air-gapped poC we can write to an internal S3-compatible store that you manage. 02:42 Mark Johnson: Are logs tamper-evident? We need chain-of-custody controls. 02:46 Samir Patel: We provide options: append-only object store plus optional integrity hashes signed by a key. We can also integrate with your WORM storage or use object-lock features on S3 to enforce immutability. We'll include a reference doc. 03:02 Daniel Ruiz: How about RBAC — mapping our AD groups to roles, and privilege separation for dev vs prod? 03:08 Leah Chen: We support SAML 2.0 and OIDC for SSO; you can map assertions/groups to our RBAC roles. For Private deployments you can choose to have the auth service federate to your IdP, and we also support SCIM for group sync. Role granularity is per-route and per-model; we can restrict model deploys, infra ops, and API keys separately. 03:28 Priya Kapoor: Do you support multi-tenant isolation inside one VPC? We have multiple business units using the same infra but need tenancy separation. 03:34 Maya Rodriguez: Yes, we support tenant isolation via namespace segmentation — logically separate routes, per-tenant model stores, and network segmentation using separate subnets and security groups. For strict isolation we recommend separate VPCs or separate clusters. 03:48 Mark Johnson: Network: ingress and egress concerns. We want to lock down outbound to only required endpoints, e.g., pull from our internal object store and contact our KMS only. Does Redwood runtime require external access for health checks or telemetry? 04:02 Leah Chen: For Private we can turn off outbound telemetry. We have two modes: fenced (no outbound to internet) and connected (managed control plane). In fenced mode all images and model artifacts are pre-staged in your registry and runtime operates without internet. For managed control-plane deployments there is limited outbound to Redwood control plane for heartbeat and license, but you can opt for proxying or egress via customer NAT. 04:24 Daniel Ruiz: So for air-gapped, nothing leaves the network. How do you handle image updates and CVE patching then? 04:30 Maya Rodriguez: Updates are done via offline bundles — we provide signed tarballs you import into your registry. We also provide CVE feeds and advisory notes; you can apply patches on your schedule. 04:39 Aisha Bello: Firewalling — our policy requires stateful inspection and ability to inspect TLS. If everything is TLS, can we do TLS interception? Any concerns about certificate pinning? 04:50 Leah Chen: You can perform TLS interception at the boundary, but for client-server mutual TLS we support mTLS between components if you want to avoid interception. We support custom certs, cert rotation, and mutual TLS for critical channels. 05:05 Mark Johnson: On egress, do you do DNS lookups externally? We need to control DNS resolution to avoid exfiltration. 05:11 Samir Patel: Redwood runtime can be configured to use your internal DNS resolvers only. We can also disable recursive resolution or incorporate DNS policies at the cluster level. 05:21 Daniel Ruiz: What about data residency — we need keys and PII to never leave EU region. How do you enforce region locks? 05:29 Leah Chen: For hosted that is a configuration, but for Private it's simpler: all data stores and compute live in your region and under your control. For Dedicated we can pin capacity in region and ensure models and artifacts are stored regionally. We'll include a short doc mapping of which components may contact Redwood control plane in connected modes. 05:49 Priya Kapoor: Can you show example network diagrams — subnets, nat gateways, firewall rules? 05:55 Maya Rodriguez: Yes, opening my screen — this is a typical VPC layout: public subnet for load balancer only; private subnets for runtime; management plane in a separate management VPC peered with data VPC; KMS endpoints in private subnets or via VPC endpoints; S3/R2 or object stores via VPC endpoints. 06:20 (screen share, brief pause) 06:30 Maya Rodriguez: For firewall rules we suggest deny-by-default and allow-specific for: outbound to your KMS endpoints on TCP 443, internal registry on 5000/443, NTP to internal NTP servers, no external DNS except via your internal resolvers, and block all unexpected egress. 06:47 Daniel Ruiz: How about deep packet inspection and IDS — any hooks to forward mirrored traffic or telemetry? 06:52 Leah Chen: You can mirror traffic at the network layer to your IDS. We also emit audit logs and some runtime metrics that can be forwarded to your IDS/monitoring. For packet-level inspection you'd use your network appliances. 07:06 Mark Johnson: Compliance evidence — can you provide SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 certs and also your penetration test results? 07:14 Samir Patel: Yes, we'll share SOC2 Type II, ISO scope and the pen test summary (redacted) under an NDA. We'll upload to your secure portal. 07:22 Aisha Bello: NDA is already in place per the RFP. 07:25 Priya Kapoor: On RBAC again — separation for service accounts vs human users. Do you allow issuing short-lived API keys tied to OIDC tokens? 07:33 Leah Chen: Yes, we support short-lived tokens and ephemeral keys. We recommend not using long-lived service keys; instead we use a token broker pattern integrated with your IdP to mint tokens per session. 07:44 Daniel Ruiz: Any side channels where model prompts might be sent to telemetry or Redwood-hosted services? We need guarantees that prompts don't leave the cluster. 07:53 Maya Rodriguez: In Private fenced mode, prompts and inference stay entirely on your data plane. In connected modes, logs and sampling telemetry can be sent with opt-in. We'll provide a configuration checklist to ensure no accidental telemetry. 08:08 Mark Johnson: For audit trails we need baked-in correlation IDs to trace a user request through to model execution and storage. 08:15 Leah Chen: We emit request IDs across the stack and they are included in logs and model execution traces. We can annotate logs with your internal user principal and correlation IDs on ingress. 08:27 Daniel Ruiz: Firewall specifics — do you support egress proxying through a customer HTTP proxy with auth? 08:33 Samir Patel: Yes, we support HTTP(S) proxy configuration for egress including NTLM/Basic where required — we recommend TLS-intercept or mTLS for stronger controls. 08:43 Priya Kapoor: What about PKI management — can you use our internal CA for service certs? 08:48 Leah Chen: Absolutely. We can provision service certs from your internal CA and support cert rotation via ACME or your cert management workflows; for HSM-backed signing we can wire to your CA endpoints. 08:59 Daniel Ruiz: Any hardcoded telemetry endpoints we should be aware of? 09:05 Maya Rodriguez: No hardcoded endpoints; all control-plane endpoints are configurable and for Private we can map them to private IPs. 09:12 Priya Kapoor: Let's talk on network ACLs vs security groups — which do you recommend? 09:18 Leah Chen: Security groups for instance-level control and NACLs for subnet-level defense in depth. We recommend both with deny-by-default NACLs when available. Also enforce AWS VPC endpoints for S3 and KMS to keep traffic in the backbone. 09:36 Mark Johnson: For the on-prem air-gapped PoC, what is minimal infra footprint and expected GPU/CPU needs? 09:43 Maya Rodriguez: Minimal PoC: 3 control plane nodes, 3 worker nodes with 1 GPU each depending on model size, internal registry, object store, and HSM/KMS endpoint. We'll send a sizing guide with a few example model footprints; this will be part of the deliverables. 10:02 Daniel Ruiz: Are there any ports that the runtime opens dynamically that we should be aware of? 10:08 Leah Chen: Mostly static ports — API 443, internal gRPC 7000-7010 range for inter-node comms, metrics on 9100 (optional). We'll provide exact ports; for strict lock-down you can run in pod-level hostPort mode with CNI policies. 10:26 Aisha Bello: From compliance: can you support audit-playback for incident response? For example replay a user session with all inputs redacted. 10:35 Samir Patel: We can export execution traces and logs. Inputs can be redacted at ingest, or you can keep a redacted copy for forensics. We'll document recommended retention and redaction patterns. 10:46 Priya Kapoor: One risk: model artifacts sometimes contain training data identifiers — can we ensure artifact scanning and classification before import? 10:54 Leah Chen: We have pre-ingest hooks and scanning — you can run your own scanners in the registry pipeline, or we can run a policy evaluation step that blocks artifacts failing checks. 11:06 Mark Johnson: Good. For governance we need SLA language around security incidents. Does Redwood do incident notification windows and post-mortem sharing? 11:15 Samir Patel: Yes — for Dedicated and Private enterprise customers we include security incident SLAs in the contract: 24-hour acknowledgment and action windows, with a post-mortem within 7 days. We'll include the standard wording in the draft contract. 11:26 Daniel Ruiz: Is there a recommended network layout for multi-region DR? 11:31 Maya Rodriguez: Yes, dual-region clusters with cross-region replication for model artifacts and asynchronous replication for logs to a cold archive. We'll include a reference architecture for DR. 11:41 Priya Kapoor: Any gotchas with KMS endpoints in private subnets — like requirement for egress to AWS KMS public endpoints? 11:48 Leah Chen: If you use managed KMS you can use VPC endpoints (AWS KMS supports VPC endpoints for most operations) or bring an HSM in your network. We'll map exact API endpoints and firewall rules. 11:57 Mark Johnson: Great — I think we've covered the main concerns. Let's recap next steps. 12:02 Samir Patel: Recap: we'll share SOC2/ISO docs, network diagram and firewall rule set, on-prem checklist and sizing, and schedule a 2-hour architecture workshop. 12:12 Priya Kapoor: Thanks, that works. We'll review and get dates back to you. 12:16 Mark Johnson: Appreciate the level of detail. 12:20 (call ends)
